item.content:encoded:
What I'm about to say has been stated over and over across the years, but it bears repeating (as the problems only become more glaring as time passes, yet this continues to climb in ratings):

long post is long
– hide block

There are serious issues here, and there are many. We have unnecessarily specific Special Containment Procedures, alternative measurement in parentheses (and it's imperial), breaks in clinical tone, copying SCP-173's "moved to X on Y" (and it's a Discovery before the Description, to boot), "seems to be", containment procedures in the Description, terminating employees of any clearance should they interact with it without permission, etc.

I also found File 256b to be poorly formatted and difficult to read. Most of it is a gauntlet of well-trodden early site tropes, which I'll list in the order they appear: Foundation personnel behaving unprofessionally so as to drive the plot, SCP Decommissioning, more than one employee going crazy (to death), and a blatant Note At The End That Explains Everything. There are also some genuine attempts at portraying scientific explanations and information security in a reasonable way — I'll admit — but the rest just brings it down.

I don't actually think this is in need of a modern rewrite. Whether the article's real truth is the "ghost in the machine" or the double fake-out, I personally found File 256b cliched, uninteresting, and padded in length, and just don't think a rewrite could serve to fix it.

item.title: Re: CALL FOR REVIEW
item.content:encoded:
SCP-256 is contained within a cubic chamber 3 m (10 ft) on a side, with 1 m (3 ft) thick walls composed of a mixture of brick and rubberized layers, with two conductive rods sticking out 18 cm (7 in) from the walls to either side of the entrance.

Downvote. I have never seen a SCP that included both metric and imperial measurements. As the Foundation runs solely on metric, the inclusion of imperial measurements is unnecessary. They are also wrong; metric doesn't nicely fit into imperial, and visa versa. One of those pairs should have decimal points in there somewhere: 1m=/=3ft. It's close enough for a good estimation, but I wouldn't build something using an estimation, especially a containment chamber.

item.title: Re: CALL FOR REVIEW
item.content:encoded:
This earns an instant downvote from me for this part right here:

Moved to Site 76 on 03-02-2007.

Not only is it blatantly ripping of 173, but it's doing it badly. You should never, and I mean

NEVER

put how or when it was obtained before the actual description. It's one of the Several Deadly Sins of SCPdom for me, which include:

  • Redaction in the containment procedures
  • Obvious Mary-Sue self inserts
  • Claiming that something is uncontainable
  • Having nonsenscial experimental, supplemental or interview logs

Speaking of that last point… I honestly don't see the purpose of the log. I literally cannot grok why it is there at all. It seems like it was put there to tell a story completely different from the main object.

Also, just to complete the Arson, Murder and Jaywalking trope, the fact that there are imperial measurements in here at all, even if they are to explain the measurements in metric, are baffling to me. These people are scientists, not chem students. They don't need to be talked down to like this, and most of them can probably do conversions on their head.

TL;DR Don't like it, -1.

E: One last point. "Does the Black Moon Howl" used to be chilling. Now, for me, all it conjures up are images of that Three Wolf Moon t-shirt. It is a laughably overused meme, both in and out of universe. If we got some context as to what the hell it actually meant, then I might actually care about it.

For another example of this, who remembers the pattern screamers? They were only used in a few articles by a user that has since left the wiki, but they still left a big enough impression to make us wonder what the hell they are or were. They were 'does the black moon howl' done correctly, because they were never overused and were always mysterious. By contrast… well, look at O5 Command's Front Page. DTBMH became so ubiquitous that they turned it into a joke. After reading half the responses on there, I could never take it seriously again.

So, another reason I dislike this article.

item.title: CALL FOR REVIEW
item.content:encoded:
SCP-256 is up for review!

Summary:

SCP-256 is at its most basic an anomalous typewriter contained within an insulated room that exhibits a number of bizarre qualities. There's mention early on of they keys themselves being stationary, the wheel roll being replaced with concave copper discs, and the object reacting negatively to conductive objects that enter its testing chamber.

Alone this would hardly warrant its own article, but the meat of this one comes in the addendum, titled "file 256b". What makes this article so interesting is that it's another example of a "Does the black moon howl?" article, where the reader is given a more in-depth look at some of the Foundation's inner workings by appearing to access a terminal and observe additional information. The reader, then, is left to infer who the individual accessing the terminal was, which is a point most interesting in this article.

To sum up the file, the idea is that a group of individuals, civilians, in fact, were under the impression that their daughter/girlfriend1 is trapped within the typewriter. Furthermore, you're led to believe that the previous site director was allowing these civilians into Site 76 for the purpose of interacting with SCP-256.

Reading on, you see that the original director, General Gerhart, has recently become in some way indisposed2, and a General Trent has taken his place. A subordinate, Edward Berstrom, goes into some detail about information not available in the original article, such as that the typewriter emits EMR similar to an oscilloscope picking up a human voice, and that 256 somehow emits audio, as well. Additionally, Berstrom notes that the individuals all believed that bringing metal near SCP-256 somehow causes it pain, and that in one instance doing so almost "killed" it. Berstrom makes his skepticism evident throughout.

At the very end you see the terminal user, whose identity remains a mystery, find and kill the new replacement director, General Trent, while causing a number of catastrophes along the way. The file ends with the ever ominous:

Does the black moon howl?

>logoff Override BaseCommand *1-0001

Goodnight, Director ██████████.

At the end, there are more questions asked than answered, leaving the reader uncomfortable and uncertain about the nature of the object, and the events that play out in the file.

The Good

This is a cool fucking story. A lot of little nuances here and there, that really draw you in and make you crave more. It's a very classic article with a lot of classic ideas and themes, like individuals within the Foundation misusing their position for various reasons, or individuals become eliminated due to some mishandling or shortcoming. The core idea is fairly uninteresting, but that is more than made up for by the depth of what comes after.

The Bad:

This thing is a mess, though, and starting to show its age. The file log, which is by far the most important feature of the article, is relatively disjointed and hard to read. From a format perspective, this could easily be in a far better way, one that would make it easier to digest. Additionally the content, while good, is getting a little old. The use of a "General" for Site Director is more or less completely discarded at this point (although that's not to say it can't be done), and many of the terms used in the containment procedures are out of date. While there are some cool ideas in there, the cool ideas are all generally muddled and difficult to approach, and would be better suited if they were not hindered by some of the strange formatting decisions.

Reviewer's Thoughts:

I really like this article. I might even say I love it. But like any sensible person in a loving relationship, even I'm not naive enough to believe that my significant other isn't riddled with flaws. With articles, however, there is a means to improve your SO, and that's by reviewing it3!

My thoughts on how to improve 256 can be condensed into three words: Clean it up. It's just messy, and generally unorganized, and could use an overhaul from a formatting point of view. The file itself is of particular note, considering its importance in the overall scheme of the piece. I think an author could probably maintain most of the central themes of the article, and be fine by going after the format and organization specifically. Were this to be done, I believe your end result would be a piece that's creepy, well thought out, and has a format screw that isn't over the top, and does exactly what it's supposed to do; create intrigue.

So those are my thoughts! Leave yours in the comments below this comment and let us know what you think. This article is nearly as old as the site itself, and deserves as much as we can give it. If you have anything you think could improve the article, please don't hesitate to speak up!

Footnotes
1. It doesn't say girlfriend, just that the individual was romantically involved with the object.
2. See: dead.
3. Notice: Don't try to review your significant other IRL.

I feel the measurement conversion could be a bit more exact. Not anything major probably just a decimal place.

with two conductive rods sticking out

Rather than conductive the material could probably be specified. Also, "sticking" could probably something more clinical such as "positioned."

SCP-256 is similar to a typewriter in most respects, except that the keys are fixed in position, rather than connected to levers, and instead of a rollbar and most of the machinery that should be present, two concave copper discs stand on either end, facing inward, 38 cm (15 in) apart.

This entire sentence feels a bit awkward and not quite the right tone. As a matter of fact the tone feels off through most of the description, but particularly here.

all unauthorized personnel regardless of clearance level must immediately evacuate the chamber. Those who fail to comply are to be terminated at once, again, regardless of security clearance.

Could probably just say "regardless of security clearance" once.

These points didn't really detract too much from the article though. Upvoted.
